headings.title: Introduction to Nutrition in HIV Management
headings.content: Nutrition plays a critical role in the comprehensive care of people living with HIV. The virus and the immune response to it increase energy expenditure while often reducing food intake. Good nutrition helps maintain body weight, preserves lean muscle mass, and supports the effectiveness of antiretroviral therapy. Clinical observation shows that well-nourished patients tolerate medications better and experience fewer opportunistic infections. Addressing dietary needs early in the disease course prevents rapid progression to malnutrition and wasting syndrome.

headings.title: Nutritional Goals and Requirements
headings.content:
Dietary planning for HIV management aims to maintain optimal body composition and support immune function. Energy requirements increase by about 10 percent during asymptomatic stages and up to 30 percent during symptomatic stages or active infections. Protein needs are also elevated to prevent muscle wasting and repair tissues. 

- **Asymptomatic stage**: Increase daily energy intake by 10 percent above normal requirements.
- **Symptomatic stage**: Increase daily energy intake by 20 to 30 percent.
- **Pediatric infection**: Increase energy intake by 10 to 30 percent to support normal growth and development.

headings.title: Macronutrient and Micronutrient Management
headings.content:
Macronutrients supply essential energy and cellular building blocks, whereas micronutrients regulate metabolic pathways and immune defense. 

| Nutrient Type | Primary Role in HIV Care | Common Sources |
| --- | --- | --- | 
| Carbohydrates | Provide readily available energy | Maize, yam, rice, millet |
| Proteins | Repair tissues and maintain muscle mass | Beans, fish, eggs, meat, groundnuts |
| Fats | Supply concentrated energy and fatty acids | Vegetable oils, avocados, seeds |
| Micronutrients | Support immune function and combat oxidative stress | Fresh fruits and dark green vegetables |

Vitamin A, zinc, and iron deficiencies frequently worsen disease progression. However, high-dose iron supplements should be used cautiously in areas with high malaria endemicity because they can sometimes increase infection risks.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment and Monitoring
headings.content: Regular nutritional screening identifies risk factors before severe wasting occurs. Anthropometric measurements, including weight, height, and body mass index, provide objective data during clinic visits. Mid-upper arm circumference is especially useful for rapid screening in community outreach settings or malnourished adults and children. Nurses must also evaluate dietary intake, swallowing difficulties, and socioeconomic barriers to food access.

headings.title: Managing HIV-Related Symptoms and Metabolic Complications
headings.content:
Gastrointestinal symptoms often interfere with adequate food intake. Oral thrush causes painful swallowing, while persistent diarrhea reduces nutrient absorption. Managing these challenges requires practical dietary adjustments:

- **Oral thrush**: Serve soft, bland, and lukewarm foods while avoiding acidic or spicy items.
- **Nausea and vomiting**: Offer dry foods like toast or biscuits and encourage small, frequent meals.
- **Diarrhea**: Ensure adequate oral rehydration salts and avoid fatty or very sweet foods.
- **Lipodystrophy**: Balance physical activity and dietary fat intake to manage fat redistribution.

headings.title: Drug-Nutrient Interactions in Antiretroviral Therapy
headings.content: Antiretroviral medications interact with food in various ways that affect absorption and tolerance. Some drugs must be taken on an empty stomach to ensure proper uptake, whereas others require food to reduce gastrointestinal upset or enhance bioavailability. Nurses must check specific administration guidelines for every regimen. A common error is advising patients to stop their medications when food is unavailable; instead, nurses should teach safe timing strategies and help patients identify which drugs genuinely require food.

headings.title: Food Safety, Hygiene, and Water Sanitation
headings.content:
Immunocompromised individuals face a high risk of foodborne and waterborne infections due to reduced immune surveillance. Contaminated water and improperly handled food can trigger severe, prolonged diarrhea and systemic illness. Safe preparation practices form a vital barrier against opportunistic pathogens.

- **Water purification**: Boil drinking water or use certified chemical disinfectants.
- **Hand hygiene**: Wash hands thoroughly with soap before preparing or eating food.
- **Food separation**: Keep raw meats separate from cooked or ready-to-eat items.
- **Proper cooking**: Cook animal source foods thoroughly to destroy harmful bacteria and parasites.

headings.title: Counseling and Support Strategies
headings.content: Effective nutritional care goes beyond prescribing a diet list; it requires empathetic counseling tailored to local realities. Nurses must assess household food security and suggest affordable, locally available food sources. Counseling sessions should involve family members or caregivers who prepare meals. Linking patients to community-based nutritional support programs ensures long-term adherence and sustained health improvements.
